Sumter County has 28,801 people by the mid-2025 estimate, down from 32,819 in 2010 and 29,616 in 2020. Americus is both the county seat and the biggest city. Andersonville, De Soto, Leslie and Plains are the other cities. A shrinking buyer pool punishes a house with a messy tax record, which tends to sit longer than its neighbors.

Owner-held homes have a midpoint value of $120,200, and owners live in 56.6% of occupied homes. That means plenty of sellable properties are rentals or inherited houses, and some come with a tenant on a lease. The county issued just 36 building permits in 2025 against 13,653 housing units, so almost every sale is a resale.

Two county offices split the work, and a house inside Americus draws a third bill from the city. The tax commissioner is at 500 W. Lamar St., Americus. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1044, the phone is (229) 928-4530, and the counter is staffed weekdays from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m.

  • Commissioner: collects money, posts payments, takes homestead filings, handles mobile home and vehicle accounts.
  • Assessors: set fair market value and taxability, and receive returns in the winter filing window.
  • Americus finance office: sends city tax bills for parcels inside Americus.

The state revenue department's sheet for Sumter shows no local homestead breaks beyond the state's, but confirm that with the commissioner. The Tax Assessor page on the county site has contact details for the appraisal side.

The county treats December 1 as the normal due date for land, buildings and business personal property. Mobile and modular homes fall due April 1, and vehicles follow the owner's birthday. Georgia's statewide default is December 20, and a county may move it to December 1 or November 15, so the date printed on your notice settles it.

After the due date, interest runs at 1 percent each month and a 10 percent penalty applies after 90 days. A homesteaded house billed under $500 avoids the penalty. Unpaid property can be levied on, though the office says it prefers other collection methods.

Americus uses its own calendar for the city portion:

  • Two installments, September 1 and December 20.
  • Installment one is based on half the prior year's total, and installment two true-ups to the current value and millage.
  • Interest of .542% per month, built from the federal prime rate plus 3%.
  • Penalty of 5% after 120 days, plus 5% more for each further 120 days, capped at 20%.

Before you pick a closing day, ask both offices for a written payoff with an expiration date.

The Sumter County commissioners and the county Board of Education set it each year. A mill means one dollar of tax for each thousand dollars assessed. Each body takes its budget needs, subtracts revenue from other sources, and picks the rate that raises the remainder.

Two neighbors with identical values can pay different totals when only one lives inside Americus, since the city adds its own rate on top of the county and school levies. The rate itself can't be argued in a value appeal. An appeal covers taxability, value and uniformity only.

Put it in writing no later than 45 days after the notice date. A late appeal is invalid, so mail it promptly and keep proof of the date.

Owners may also declare a value each winter on a return filed between the first of January and the first of April. If the board rejects your number, a notice with its own value follows. Appeals can argue taxability, value, or fairness against similar properties. Disliking the final bill is no ground, since the commissioners and school board set the rate.

Georgia also has a refund rule. A written request for money collected in error or illegally must begin within three years of payment, and an appealed assessment brings an automatic refund when the final value is set.

Homestead is the main one. You can apply at any point once the house is your main residence, provided the form arrives by April 1 of the first year you want relief. Not applying counts as waiving it.

  • Homestead: one application, then it carries forward.
  • Freeport: business inventory, if voters in the county approved it.
  • Mobile home permit: required 30 days after permanent placement, then renewed each year from January 1 to April 1.

Dollar amounts come from the state constitution and the General Assembly, so ask the commissioner for the current numbers.

Work through these in order, ideally a few weeks before you accept an offer, so no tax bill ambushes you at the closing table. It is mostly phone calls, and each office can usually answer in one conversation if you have the parcel number ready.

  1. Pull your latest bill and note whether it covers county, school and, inside Americus, city levies.
  2. Phone the commissioner and ask which years carry an open balance on the parcel.
  3. If the house is in Americus, make the same call to the city finance office.
  4. Confirm your homestead filing is on record, since a buyer's title company will look for it.
  5. For a manufactured home, ask about the April 1 permit tax and decal.
  6. Request written payoffs with an expiration date and hand copies to your closing agent.

If a house has sat vacant or passed through an estate, expect more than one open year and plan for a longer payoff list. A cash buyer can take the property as it stands and clear those balances at closing, so you skip the repair requests and lender timelines that slow a traditional sale.

Start by collecting payoffs: one from the county for each open year and another from Americus if the house lies within the city. A delinquent account can turn into a FIFA, a lien entered in the superior court clerk's records, and a title search will show it.

The year's bill belongs to the January 1 owner, the same date used to measure fair market value. For a June sale, your settlement statement splits the cost with the buyer, and the closing agent covers any balance out of your proceeds. A manufactured home adds an April 1 permit tax and decal to the list.

Inherited houses and former rentals often hold the heaviest balances, especially where nobody opened the mail for a few years. A cash purchase can settle those in a single closing.

faqs.q: What address does the Sumter County tax commissioner use?
faqs.a: The office is at 500 W. Lamar St. in Americus, and mail goes to P.O. Box 1044. Call (229) 928-4530 or stop by weekdays from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m.

faqs.q: Is Sumter County's due date December 1 or December 20?
faqs.a: The county uses December 1 for real estate. Georgia's default is December 20 and a county may pull it earlier, so go by your notice.

faqs.q: How long can I wait to dispute a Sumter County value?
faqs.a: No more than 45 days after the date printed on your assessment notice. It must be written, and a late one is invalid.

faqs.q: Does living in Americus mean a second bill?
faqs.a: Yes. The city sends its own bill, with installments due September 1 and December 20, separate from the county's bill.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Sumter County house that owes back taxes?
faqs.a: You can. Get a payoff from the commissioner, then have the closing agent pay it out of your proceeds so the lien is released when the deed records.
